summary:
Visitors to Delaware stand under the United States federal framework in every respect that governs entry and travel documents. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU is litigating on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 refuse visas to trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, flag applicants internally under the code 'SWS25', and permit an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth to be treated as fraud and barred permanently. Checkpoint screening carries its own exposure: secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can disclose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers.

Delaware itself does not add a state-level layer of restriction. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 places Delaware in its Low-Risk States group, alongside Arizona, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, defined as jurisdictions that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specialising in their protection. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records no ban on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity for Delaware, and no Delaware statute of that kind appears in the inventory.
tangentialFactors:
Delaware's position is best read against the surrounding national pattern. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with further states imposing outright bans on facility use by gender identity and some treating trans bathroom use as a criminal offence in certain circumstances; twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has moved past theory: in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed at the Florida state capitol for using a women's restroom, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, described by rights groups as a template other legislatures are following.

The same July 2026 assessment designates four states do-not-travel for trans people, Idaho being the most recently flagged, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures. Delaware sits in the opposite group of that assessment. Foreign governments have responded to the federal document rules with public advisories: at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens, advisories that followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.
localsOnly:
Federal policy on housing transgender prisoners has shifted repeatedly and governs any trans person taken into custody in Delaware. A January 2015 ICE memo directed housing transgender immigration detainees according to gender identity, and 2016 Department of Justice guidelines forbade corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy. In 2018 the Federal Bureau of Prisons revised its Transgender Offender Manual in the opposite direction, deleting the commitment that the Transgender Executive Council would recommend housing by gender identity when appropriate and making placement a case-by-case determination in which biological sex is the initial consideration and gender identity is used only in rare cases.

For residents, the Movement Advancement Project maintains a state-by-state identity-document map setting out which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules a Delaware resident encounters depend on Delaware's own provisions as recorded there.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Movement Advancement Project equality-map page cited for Delaware's facility-use position returned HTTP 404 at the archived URL during this pass; the finding of no Delaware ban rests on the underlying map's recorded data rather than a retrievable page, and the citation remains unresolved for verification.

No Delaware-specific placement policy for transgender prisoners is documented in the sources reviewed, so the federal Bureau of Prisons framework is the only custody-housing rule that can be stated here.

The inventory contains no source on Delaware's own rules for changing gender markers on driver's licences or birth certificates; the state-level document position for Delaware is not sourced in this pass.
